Title: The altered mononuclear cell-derived cytokine response to glucose ingestion is not regulated by excess adiposity in polycystic ovary syndrome.

Journal/Date: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism (2014)

MeSH Keywords: Adiposity, Adult, Body Composition, Cross-Sectional Studies, Female, Glucose, Glucose Tolerance Test, Humans


--- ABSTRACT ---
[CONTEXT]: Excess adipose tissue is a source of inflammation. Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a proinflammatory state and is often associated with excess abdominal adiposity (AA) alone and/or frank obesity.
[OBJECTIVE]: To determine the effect of glucose ingestion on cytokine release from mononuclear cells (MNC) in women with PCOS with and without excess AA and/or obesity.
[DESIGN]: A cross-sectional study.
[SETTING]: Academic medical center.
[PATIENTS]: Twenty-three women with PCOS (seven normal weight with normal AA, eight normal weight with excess AA, eight obese) and 24 ovulatory controls (eight normal weight with normal AA, eight normal weight with excess AA, eight obese).
[INTERVENTION]: Three-hour 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT).
[MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES]: Body composition was measured by dual energy x-ray absorptiometry. Insulin sensitivity was derived from the OGTT (ISOGTT). TNFα, IL-6, and IL-1β release was measured in supernatants of cultured MNC isolated from blood samples drawn while fasting and 2 hours after glucose ingestion.
[RESULTS]: Insulin sensitivity was lower in obese subjects regardless of PCOS status and in normal-weight women with PCOS compared with normal-weight controls regardless of body composition status. In response to glucose ingestion, MNC-derived TNFα, IL-6, and IL-1β release decreased in both normal-weight control groups but failed to suppress in either normal-weight PCOS group and in obese women regardless of PCOS status. For the combined groups, the cytokine responses were negatively correlated with insulin sensitivity and positively correlated with abdominal fat and androgens.
[CONCLUSIONS]: Women with PCOS fail to suppress MNC-derived cytokine release in response to glucose ingestion, and this response is independent of excess adiposity. Nevertheless, a similar response is also a feature of obesity per se. Circulating MNC and excess adipose tissue are separate and distinct sources of inflammation in this population.

key_findings.finding: After a 75-g OGTT, cultured MNC-derived TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IL-1beta release decreased in both normal-weight control groups, but failed to suppress in both normal-weight PCOS groups and in obese subjects regardless of PCOS status. Responses correlated negatively with insulin sensitivity and positively with abdominal fat and androgens, but the authors concluded that PCOS-associated failure to suppress cytokines was independent of excess adiposity; obesity itself produced a similar abnormal response, implying separate inflammatory contributions from circulating MNCs and adipose tissue.

source_tools.relevance: Cytokines, direction of response, correlations and authors’ conclusion

key_findings.finding: A related 2014 study (PMID 24576416) used 16 PCOS women (8 lean, 8 obese) and 15 weight-matched controls (8 lean, 7 obese), with truncal fat measured by DEXA. Lean PCOS women and obese controls failed to suppress LPS-stimulated MNC IL-6 and IL-1beta after glucose ingestion, whereas obese PCOS women suppressed both cytokines. Plasma IL-6 and sVCAM-1 increased and CRP suppression was attenuated after glucose in both PCOS groups and obese controls versus lean controls. The authors concluded the systemic proatherogenic response was independent of obesity, while profound chronic inflammation in obese PCOS may cause LPS tolerance and suppress the MNC response; excess abdominal adiposity and hyperandrogenism may contribute but do not account for the PCOS alteration.

source_tools.relevance: Independent weight-matched study with IL-6/IL-1beta direction and conclusion

key_findings.finding: An earlier controlled study (PMID 15985479) included 16 PCOS women (8 lean, 8 obese) and 14 age-matched controls (8 lean, 6 obese), measured truncal fat by DEXA, and assessed LPS-stimulated MNC TNF-alpha before and 2 hours after a 75-g OGTT. TNF-alpha responses differed by weight class: obese controls and obese PCOS showed decreases, whereas lean controls and lean PCOS showed increases. Lean PCOS had greater truncal fat than lean controls. The authors interpreted abdominal adiposity and increased TNF-alpha release after hyperglycemia as contributors to insulin resistance in lean PCOS, while obese PCOS showed more chronic inflammation and possible LPS tolerance; this study supports an adiposity-related contribution but does not establish that adiposity explains the PCOS-specific alteration.

source_tools.relevance: Earlier human study, group composition, truncal-fat measure, TNF-alpha direction and nuanced conclusion
